notes.meaning: The Passover feast was approaching, and Jesus knew the time had arrived for Him to leave this world and return to the Father. Even with the cross ahead, His focus remained on His followers. He continued to love them completely, pouring out His affection to the very end of His earthly life.

The evening meal was underway, and the devil had already planted the idea of betrayal into the heart of Judas. Judas allowed greed and bitterness to take root instead of listening to his Lord. Jesus knew what was brewing, yet He remained in complete control of every moment.

Jesus knew that the Father had placed all power and authority into His hands. He was fully conscious of His divine origin and His certain return to heaven. With this complete awareness of His royal dignity, He chose to perform an astonishing act of humility.

Jesus got up from the table, took off His outer robe, and tied a servant's linen towel around His waist. He then poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples' feet, wiping them with the towel. In Bible times, washing dusty feet was the menial work of the lowest slave, yet the Lord of all did it willingly.

Jesus came to Simon Peter, who was stunned to see his Master stooping down before him. Peter asked if the Lord was truly going to wash his feet, pulling back in deep astonishment. He felt it was completely backward for the King of glory to do the work of a slave for a sinner.

Jesus answered that Peter could not understand the deeper meaning of this action right then. He promised that Peter would understand it later, after the cross and resurrection. Believers must often trust and obey Christ even when His actions seem mysterious at the moment.

Peter firmly refused, insisting that Jesus would never wash his feet. Jesus warned him that unless He washed him, Peter could have no share or fellowship with Him. Peter needed to learn that no one can belong to Christ without humbly receiving the spiritual cleansing only He can give.

When Peter realized that refusal meant being separated from Christ, his attitude changed at once. He asked Jesus to wash not just his feet, but his hands and head too. Peter's quick reaction showed his intense love for the Master, even though he still struggled to understand the lesson.

Jesus explained that someone who has taken a full bath only needs to wash their feet to be clean all over. A traveler coming home from the public bath got dusty feet along the road, needing only a quick rinse. In the Christian life, a believer is forgiven once for all at salvation, but still needs daily cleansing from everyday sins.

Jesus noted that not all of them were clean, because He already knew who was going to betray Him. He washed Judas's feet right alongside the others, but Judas had refused to receive inward cleansing. Outward religious actions can never change a heart that chooses darkness.

After washing their feet, Jesus put His outer robe back on and returned to His place at the table. He asked the disciples if they understood the true meaning of what He had done. He wanted them to look past the physical water to the spiritual lesson of self-giving love.

Jesus noted that they addressed Him as Teacher and Lord, and He affirmed that those titles were correct. Performing the work of a slave did not diminish His true authority or majesty. His humility showed what God's leadership really looks like.

Jesus told them that since their Lord and Teacher had washed their feet, they should wash one another's feet. He provided a living pattern of selfless service for them to copy. Followers of Jesus are called to treat each other with practical kindness and humble care.

differ.view: A few church groups, such as the Brethren and some Baptists, practice foot-washing as a literal church ordinance alongside baptism and the Lord's Supper.
Most Protestant traditions understand Jesus to be giving an example of a humble, servant-hearted attitude to guide daily life, rather than commanding a permanent church ceremony.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic Church includes foot-washing in its Holy Thursday liturgy as a symbolic reminder of Christ's charity and priestly service, rather than treating it as a sacrament.

notes.meaning: Jesus stated that a servant is not greater than his master, and a messenger is not greater than the one who sent him. If the Master was willing to do the lowliest chore, His servants have no right to act superior. Pride must never keep a Christian from serving others.

Jesus declared that knowing these truths brings no benefit unless a person actually practices them. True happiness and God's favor belong to those who put their faith into action. Real Christian maturity is measured by obedience, not just head knowledge.

Jesus clarified that His blessing would not apply to everyone in the room because He knew who was faithful and who was not. The coming betrayal was not an accident; it fulfilled Psalm 41, which warned that a close companion sharing bread would turn viciously against his friend. Even in this dark treachery, God's sovereign plan was moving forward.

Jesus revealed the betrayal beforehand so that the disciples would not lose their faith when it happened. Seeing His words come to pass would prove to them that He truly was the promised Messiah, the Lord who knows all things. Prophecy fulfilled strengthens our trust in God's word.

Jesus assured the disciples that whoever welcomes one of His messengers welcomes Him, and whoever welcomes Him welcomes God the Father. This promise comforted the faithful apostles after hearing about the coming betrayal. Their upcoming mission would carry the full authority and presence of God Himself.

Jesus felt deep sorrow in His human spirit as He formally warned the group that one of them would betray Him. The thought of treachery from a trusted friend brought real grief to His heart. He spoke plainly so that the hidden wickedness would be exposed.

The disciples looked around at each other in utter bewilderment, wondering which one of them could do such a thing. Judas had hidden his deceit so skillfully that no one pointed a finger at him. Aware of their own weaknesses, each man felt unsettled and grieved.

John, who modestly referred to himself as the disciple Jesus loved, was reclining right next to Jesus at the table. Diners leaned on low couches on their left elbow, leaving the right hand free to eat. This seating arrangement placed John right beside Jesus in an intimate position of friendship.

Simon Peter made a sign to John, nodding or gesturing for him to ask Jesus who the traitor was. Peter was eager to find out the truth, but was sitting too far away to whisper directly to Jesus. He hoped John's close place would allow him to ask quietly.

John leaned back against Jesus' chest and quietly asked the Lord to identify the betrayer. He used his close place at the meal to speak privately, without creating a scene among the others. John showed simple confidence in approaching the Lord with Peter's question.

Jesus whispered back that the traitor would be the one to whom He handed a piece of dipped bread. He then dipped the morsel into the dish and offered it directly to Judas. In Jewish dining customs, handing bread to a guest was a gesture of special honor and care, giving Judas one final plea of love.

As soon as Judas took the bread, Satan took full control of his hardened heart. Jesus then told Judas to go and do his work quickly. This was not permission to sin, but an expression of Jesus' total readiness to face the cross without hesitation.

None of the other disciples at the table understood what Jesus meant by His words to Judas. Because Judas managed the money bag for the group, some assumed he was sent to buy supplies for the feast or to give an offering to the poor. They remained completely unaware of the evil deal Judas was about to carry out.

As soon as Judas took the piece of bread, he stepped out of the room into the night. It was physically dark outside, but his exit also marked the deep spiritual darkness swallowing his life. He walked away from Jesus, the Light of the World, to deliver Him up to death.

Once Judas had departed, Jesus announced that the Son of Man was now glorified, and God was glorified in Him. The wheels of His suffering were turning, and the cross would reveal God's great justice, holiness, and mercy. Because the Son honored the Father through His sacrifice, the Father would immediately honor the Son through the resurrection.

Jesus gently addressed the disciples as His little children, telling them He would only be with them a short time longer. He said that where He was going, they could not come right now. He used this tender family language to comfort them and prepare them for the pain of His departure.

Jesus gave His followers a new commandment: to love one another just as He had loved them. The standard was new because it was modeled on His own self-sacrificing love. He explained that this genuine love for each other would be the identifying badge proving to the whole world that they belonged to Him.

Simon Peter asked where Jesus was going, troubled by the idea of being left behind. Jesus replied that Peter could not follow Him at that moment, but would follow Him later on. Jesus was walking the solitary path of the cross, but Peter would one day lay down his life for the gospel as well.

Peter pressed further, asking why he could not follow Jesus immediately, and insisted he was ready to die for Him. Peter's feelings were sincere, but he was completely blind to his own human weakness. He relied on his own courage rather than the power of God's Spirit.

Jesus gently challenged Peter's confident boast and delivered a sobering warning. He told Peter that before the rooster crowed the next morning, Peter would deny even knowing Him three times. This sad prediction proved that Jesus knows our hearts far better than we know ourselves.
